title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (7 of 7)
hook: a tree with its roots in the sky, the knots of the heart, and a boy set free from death
carry: choose the good over the pleasant
tomorrow: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (1 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, uttishthata: arise, awake. The path is sharp as a razor's edge, and the wise turn the gaze around to find a flame without smoke.

A boy was given to Death by an angry father. He waited three nights hungry at Death's door, turned down every pleasure in the world, and asked the question Death itself didn't want to answer. A story like that could end with a bargain lost, or a little time won before Death comes back. Not this one. In the Katha's last pages, Death finishes teaching. And the boy walks out of Death's house free.
screen: `A BOY AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `NOT A BARGAIN LOST.` → `THE BOY WALKS OUT FREE.`

segments.voice: Near the end, Yama gives three last pictures. First, a tree: the eternal ashvattha, a sacred fig, with its roots above and its branches below. The world hangs down from what's above it, like a tree upside down. The Gita opens chapter fifteen with the same tree. Second, yoga. When the five senses are still, with the mind, and the intellect doesn't stir, that's called the highest state. Yama defines yoga as that firm holding of the senses. Not a pose. A steadiness: the reins from the chariot, held firm. Third, the heart. When all the desires that dwell in the heart are let go, the mortal becomes immortal, and reaches Brahman here. When all the knots of the heart are cut, even in this life, the mortal becomes immortal. Not escape from the world; a heart with its knots untied. Then the last verse. Nachiketa, having received this knowledge from Death, and the whole method of yoga, reached Brahman, free of stain and free of death. And so will anyone, the text says, who knows the self this way. That's the week. Old cows and a boy's question. Three nights at Death's door. Peace with his father, the fire, and the third wish. The two paths, the good and the pleasant. The self not born, not dying. The chariot. Arise, awake. And the knots of the heart, cut.
screen: `THE TREE WITH ROOTS ABOVE.` · `YOGA: THE SENSES HELD STILL.` · `THE KNOTS OF THE HEART, CUT.` · `NACHIKETA, FREE OF DEATH.` · then, large: `THE TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Bring your attention to the center of your chest and notice if there's a knot there right now: a worry, a want, a grudge. Don't try to cut it; breathe toward it, the way you'd breathe on cold hands, and let the senses go still one at a time, eyes resting, ears resting, the body quiet. That steadiness, the Katha says, is yoga; if the knot loosens even a little, notice that.
Ashvattha, the sacred fig with roots above and branches below. Nachiketa chose the good, learned from Death, and walked out free. That's the Katha.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Tomorrow, twelve verses and one syllable: om. That's day two hundred fifty-two.

what a scholar hears: Katha 2.3.11 (tam yogam iti manyante sthiram indriya-dharanam) is often cited by scholars as an early technical use of 'yoga'; 2.3.1 parallels Gita 15.1.

chat.says: How does the Katha end? Did Death keep the boy after all?
options: No. Nachiketa learned from Death and walked out free of death.
Yes. He learned the truth, then had to stay in Death's house.
No. Death sent him home early, before teaching him anything more.
chat.meaning: Having received this knowledge from Death, and the whole method of yoga, Nachiketa reached Brahman, free of stain and free of death.

Ashvattha.meaning: the sacred fig, pictured with roots above and branches below

yoga.meaning: here: the firm, steady holding of the senses

Brahman.meaning: the tradition's word for the ultimate reality, the ground of everything

Nachiketa.meaning: the boy who went to Death's house and asked his question
